title: Bits, Merges and Fronts
focus: The XOR family, merging k streams, the hardest common tree question, and BFS from many sources at once.

cards.title: Bit Manipulation
patterns: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit
cards.trigger: Pairs that cancel, subsets of a small set, or a constraint on space that forbids a hash map.
cards.recall: From memory: the four identities. What is `x ^ x`, `x ^ 0`, what does `n & (n-1)` do, and what does `n & -n` isolate? Then write the single-number solution.
useWhen: Single number, or two single numbers among pairs
Count set bits, power of two check
Subset enumeration over up to about 20 elements
Missing number via XOR of indices and values
Sum of two integers without the plus operator
template: x ^ x == 0;  x ^ 0 == x;  xor is commutative and associative
n & (n - 1)      # clears the lowest set bit  -> power of two iff result is 0
n & -n           # isolates the lowest set bit
# Single number: every other value appears twice
for x in nums: r ^= x
# Two singles: xor everything, then split by any bit where they differ
# Enumerate every subset of a bitmask
while sub: sub = (sub - 1) & mask     # all submasks of mask
keyInsights: XOR is its own inverse, which is why pairs vanish and order does not matter
`n & -n` relies on two's complement. It is the standard way to isolate a differing bit for the two-singles split
Python integers are arbitrary precision, so 32-bit problems need an explicit mask and a sign fix-up
cards.trap: 'Every element appears three times except one.' XOR no longer cancels. You count bits modulo 3, or track two accumulators. Have the bit-counting version ready.

cards.title: Merge K Sorted
cards.trigger: Several already-sorted sequences, and you must interleave them into one.
cards.recall: Write the heap version from memory. Then answer: why is O(N log k) better than concatenate-and-sort at O(N log N), and when is it actually not?
useWhen: Merge k sorted linked lists or arrays
External sort, merging sorted chunks from disk
Smallest range covering an element from each list
Kth smallest in a sorted matrix
Merging time-ordered event streams
template: heapq.heappush(h, (node.val, i, node))   # i breaks ties, nodes are not comparable
# Divide and conquer: merge pairs, halving the list count each round
lists = [merge_two(lists[i], lists[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(lists) else None)
return lists[0] if lists else None

complexity.time: O(N log k), N = total items

keyInsights: The heap only ever holds k items, one per list. That is where the log k instead of log N comes from
The tie-breaker index is not optional in Python. Without it the heap tries to compare ListNode objects and raises
Divide and conquer matches the complexity with O(1) extra space, and is often the answer they prefer for linked lists
cards.trap: 'The lists are on disk and do not fit in memory.' The heap version streams and is the right answer. Concatenate-and-sort is not even possible. Say that.

cards.title: Maximum Path Sum
cards.trigger: A path that may start and end anywhere, and values may be negative.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer both traps at once: why clamp negative children to zero, and why can the value you return to the parent not include both children?
useWhen: Binary tree maximum path sum
Longest univalue path, longest zigzag path
Diameter with weighted edges
Maximum sum of a subtree, a different but neighbouring shape
Any tree problem where the answer bends
template: l = max(gain(node.left),  0)      # a negative arm is worse than no arm
best = max(best, node.val + l + r)   # RECORD: the bent path
return node.val + max(l, r)          # RETURN: one arm only
#   diameter        -> record l + r,          return 1 + max(l, r)
#   univalue path   -> arms count only when child.val == node.val
keyInsights: Initialise `best` to negative infinity, not zero, or an all-negative tree returns a wrong 0
Clamping at zero is the same as saying the empty extension is always available
This is the archetype of the record-versus-return pattern. Recognise it and three other hard problems become easy
cards.trap: 'The path must contain at least one node' versus 'may be empty'. Those are different answers on an all-negative tree. Ask before you code.

cards.title: Word Break DP
cards.trigger: Can this string be cut into pieces that all come from a given set.
cards.recall: Say what `dp[i]` means, then write the double loop from memory. Then answer: which loop is the split point, and why is the dictionary a set rather than a list?
useWhen: Word break, and word break II which returns all sentences
Concatenated words, palindrome partitioning
Decode a string under a set of valid tokens
Minimum cuts to split a string into valid pieces
Any 'can this be segmented' phrasing
template: # dp[i] = True if s[:i] can be fully segmented
max_len = max(map(len, ws)) if ws else 0
dp[0] = True                        # empty prefix is segmentable
for j in range(max(0, i - max_len), i):   # j is the last split point
if dp[j] and s[j:i] in ws:
# Return all sentences: memoise on the start index and return lists
out += [s[start:end] + (' ' + rest).rstrip() for rest in go(end)]
keyInsights: Capping the inner loop at the longest dictionary word turns O(n^2) into O(n * L), which matters on long strings
A list dictionary makes each lookup O(k). A set makes it O(1). That is the difference between passing and timing out
The all-sentences variant is exponential in output size, so memoising on start index is the only sane structure
cards.trap: 'The dictionary has a hundred thousand words with long shared prefixes.' Now a trie beats the set, because you walk the string and the trie together.

cards.title: Multi-Source BFS
patterns: Seed the queue with every source
One level equals one time step
cards.trigger: Spreading from many starting points at once, and you need the time until everything is covered.
cards.recall: Write rotting oranges from memory. Then answer: why is seeding all sources at once correct, rather than running BFS from each source and taking the minimum?
useWhen: Rotting oranges, fire or infection spread
Distance to the nearest zero or nearest gate
Walls and gates, shortest distance from any exit
Map of highest peak, or any 'distance from the nearest of a set'
As many rounds as it takes, count the rounds
template: if grid[r][c] == 2: q.append((r, c))   # EVERY source, seeded at once
for _ in range(len(q)):                    # one whole level = one minute
nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
keyInsights: Seeding all sources is equivalent to adding a virtual super-source with zero-cost edges to each. That is the one-line justification
One BFS over all sources is O(V + E). Separate BFS per source is O(S * (V + E)). On a grid full of sources that is quadratic
The `while q and fresh` guard stops you counting a final empty minute, which is the classic off-by-one here
cards.trap: 'Some cells have different spread speeds.' It is no longer unweighted, so BFS is wrong. That is Dijkstra with a multi-source seed.
